book.title: Vestibular Disorders: BPPV and Vestibular Hypofunction

blocks.text: The vestibular system in the inner ear senses head movement and gravity. It keeps the eyes stable during head movement (vestibulo-ocular reflex, VOR) and helps balance.

items: **Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)**: tiny calcium crystals (otoconia) move into a semicircular canal, usually the posterior canal. Head position changes then cause brief spinning vertigo. It is the most common cause of vertigo [Ref – to verify].
**Unilateral vestibular hypofunction**: one inner ear or nerve works poorly, for example after vestibular neuritis. Causes dizziness with head movement, imbalance and blurred vision during movement.
**Central causes** (stroke, MS, tumour) can mimic these and must not be missed.

rows: Episodes triggered by position (lying down, rolling, looking up)
Continuous for days, then gradual improvement
Nausea, imbalance; hearing normal in neuritis
Other neurological signs, severe imbalance, new headache
Vertigo suggests vestibular; light-headedness suggests cardiovascular causes
What triggers it? Rolling in bed, looking up?
How long does each episode last?
Seconds: BPPV; minutes to hours: migraine or Ménière disease; days: neuritis or stroke
Double vision, slurred speech, numbness, weakness, unable to walk?

blocks.text: Oculomotor exam (smooth pursuit, saccades, spontaneous and gaze-evoked nystagmus), head impulse test, positional tests, balance and gait, cervical screen, orthostatic BP.

blocks.text: E2. Supine roll test (horizontal canal BPPV)

Supine with the head flexed about 30 degrees; quickly rotate the head 90 degrees to each side. Horizontal nystagmus on both sides suggests horizontal canal BPPV; the direction and intensity help identify the side [Ref – to verify].

Patient fixes gaze on your nose. Hold the head and make a small, quick, unpredictable rotation (about 10 to 20 degrees). Normal: eyes stay on target. Positive: eyes move with the head, then a corrective "catch-up" saccade back to the target, indicating hypofunction on the side the head was turned toward.
E4. HINTS examination (acute continuous vertigo, done by trained clinicians)

**H**ead **I**mpulse, **N**ystagmus type, **T**est of **S**kew. In acute continuous vertigo, a normal head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus or a skew deviation suggest a central cause such as stroke [Ref – to verify].

blocks.label: COMMON STUDENT TRAP
body: In a patient with acute continuous vertigo, a normal head impulse test is worrying, not reassuring. It suggests the inner ear is working and the problem may be central.

rows: Days of vertigo, positive head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus
Episodes lasting hours with hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness
Neurological signs, severe imbalance, HINTS central
Neck pain linked to dizziness, diagnosis of exclusion

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Vertigo with double vision, dysarthria, dysphagia, numbness, weakness, unable to stand or walk
New severe headache or neck pain with vertigo
Down-beating or pure vertical nystagmus without positional pattern
Positional vertigo that does not respond to several correct manoeuvres

steps: **Brief positional episodes?** Dix-Hallpike and roll test; treat the identified canal.
**Continuous dizziness worse with head movement, positive head impulse?** Vestibular hypofunction: vestibular rehabilitation.

items: Start as for the right Dix-Hallpike: head turned 45 degrees right, lie back with the head extended. Hold 30 to 60 seconds or until nystagmus stops.
Turn the head 90 degrees to the left (now 45 degrees left), keeping extension. Hold 30 to 60 seconds.
Roll the patient onto the left side, turning the head a further 90 degrees so the face points toward the floor. Hold 30 to 60 seconds.
Bring the patient up to sitting with the head still turned left and chin slightly tucked.
Re-test after a few minutes or at the next visit. Repeat if still positive.

blocks.text: Post-manoeuvre restrictions are generally not necessary [Ref – to verify].
Horizontal canal BPPV is treated with roll manoeuvres (for example barbecue roll) instead.

rows: Look at a letter on a card at arm's length; move head side to side while keeping it in focus
Faster speed, busy background, standing, walking
Repeat movements that provoke mild dizziness
A few repetitions, several times daily
Feet together, tandem, eyes closed, foam
Dynamic tasks, head turns while walking

blocks.text: Symptom rule: mild, short-lived dizziness during exercises is expected and needed; dizziness lasting hours means reduce dose.

Medications that suppress the vestibular system (for example some antiemetics and sedatives) may help in the first days but can slow adaptation if used long-term [Ref – to verify]. Coordinate with the doctor.
Dizziness Handicap Inventory, positional tests, dynamic visual acuity, head impulse test, balance (Functional Gait Assessment).

items: **What nystagmus suggests right posterior canal BPPV on Dix-Hallpike?** Up-beating torsional nystagmus with the top of the eye beating toward the right (lower) ear, short latency, lasting under a minute.
**Why is a positive head impulse test reassuring in acute vertigo?** It points to a peripheral vestibular cause rather than central.
**What exercise trains the VOR?** Gaze stabilisation (VOR x1).
**Dizziness lasting hours with tinnitus and hearing loss?** Ménière disease: ENT referral.
**When do you call emergency services?** Vertigo with any central neurological sign or new severe headache.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Distinguish BPPV, vestibular hypofunction and central causes.
Perform and interpret the Dix-Hallpike and head impulse tests.
Prescribe gaze stabilisation and balance exercises.

sections.A: Kaan ke andar vestibular system sar ki movement aur gravity mehsoos karta hai aur nazar aur balance ko stable rakhta hai. BPPV mein chhote crystals ghalat naali mein chale jate hain.
sections.B: BPPV: position badalne (letna, karwat, upar dekhna) par chand second ka chakkar. Hypofunction: lagataar unsteadiness, sar ghumane par barhti.
sections.C: Kya kamra ghoomta hai (vertigo) ya sirf halka-pan (dil ya BP), har episode kitni der, aur kya sunne mein tabdeeli hai.
sections.D: Aankhon ki movements, nystagmus, head impulse test aur balance.
sections.E: Dix-Hallpike (posterior canal) aur roll test (horizontal canal) chakkar aur nystagmus paida karte hain.
sections.F: BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Meniere aur central (dimagh) wajahein ka farq table mein hai.
sections.G: Chakkar ke saath double vision, bolne ya nigalne mein masla, sunn-pan, kamzori ya khade na ho sakna: stroke ka shak, emergency.
sections.H: Pehle central signs screen karein. Chhote positional episodes ho to Dix-Hallpike aur roll test; positive ho to repositioning.
sections.I: Epley manoeuvre posterior canal BPPV ke crystals wapas sahi jagah le jata hai.
sections.J: Hypofunction ke liye gaze stabilisation (VOR x1), habituation aur balance exercises.
sections.K: Chakkar dabane wali dawayein shuru mein madad kar sakti hain lekin lambe arsay tak recovery dheemi karti hain.
sections.M: Dizziness Handicap Inventory, positional tests, head impulse aur balance dobara dekhein.
sections.N: Sawaal hal karein. Right posterior canal BPPV mein Dix-Hallpike par up-beating torsional nystagmus hota hai.
